title: Jesus as the Messiah
subtitle: One shared title, two understandings — what al-Masih means in Islam and what “Christ” means in Christianity
summary: Islam and Christianity both call Jesus the Messiah. The title means 'anointed one' and originally described human kings and priests chosen by God. Christianity connects it to Jesus's divinity and atoning death. Islam preserves its prophetic meaning: Jesus is God's chosen Messiah and servant, sent to Israel and supported with miracles, while God alone receives worship.

seo.metaTitle: Jesus as the Messiah: What Islam Means by al-Masih
seo.metaDescription: Jesus's title of Messiah in the Quran and Christianity, and why Islam connects his honor with servanthood rather than worship.

sections.title: You Can Believe in the Messiah Without Worshiping Him
sections.body:
Islam does not ask you to abandon Jesus as Messiah. It asks whether being chosen by God makes the chosen person God. The title itself does not establish deity; the Quran places Jesus's unique mission within human prophethood.

Christians give the title a wider meaning through Jesus's death, resurrection, and divine sonship. The real discussion must examine that meaning, not pretend a dictionary settles the whole disagreement.

sections.title: Introduction: Christ Is a Title, Not a Name
sections.body:
Few words carry as much weight between Islam and Christianity as “Messiah.” In English Bibles it usually appears in its Greek-derived form, “Christ” — so often that many readers assume Christ is part of Jesus’s name. It is not a name but a title, from the Hebrew mashiach, meaning “anointed one,” rendered in Greek as christos and in Arabic as al-Masih.

Remarkably, the Quran itself uses this title for Jesus — freely, repeatedly, and with honor, bestowing it through an angelic announcement before he is even born.

But shared words can carry different meanings. When a Christian confesses “Jesus is the Christ” and a Muslim says “Isa al-Masih,” the same title is being understood in importantly different ways.

sections.title: A Shared Title Does Not Mean an Identical Mission
sections.body:
John 1:41 explains Messiah through the Greek title Christ. The word concerns anointing or appointment, not a definition of divine nature. That is why accepting the title does not by itself entail the Trinity.

Yet Christian belief is not based on the word alone. It identifies this particular Messiah through the wider New Testament story. Islam must therefore explain why it accepts Jesus's title while rejecting central parts of that story. Its answer depends on the Quran's authority to confirm and correct, examined in [Why the Quran?](/articles/why-the-quran).

sections.title: Historical Context: Anointing in Ancient Israel
sections.body:
Messiah comes from the Hebrew mashiach, "anointed one"; Christ comes from the Greek christos. In the Hebrew Bible, kings and priests could be anointed for a God-given task. The title therefore signals divine choice and mission before it says anything about divinity.

Jewish hopes later gathered around a coming ruler from David's line who would restore justice. Early Christians identified Jesus as that Messiah and interpreted his death and resurrection as the unexpected fulfillment of the role. Islam also affirms the title while defining Jesus's mission through prophecy and servanthood.

sections.title: Al-Masih Does Not Disdain to Be God's Servant
sections.body:
The Quran calls Jesus al-Masih, the Messiah, beginning with the announcement of his birth in Quran 3:45. It joins that title with honor in this world and the next. It does not explain the title through a ritual of anointing. Muslim commentators offer several explanations; [Ibn Kathir](https://quran.com/ali-imran/45/tafsirs/en-tafisr-ibn-kathir), for example, connects it with Jesus touching and healing the sick by Allah's permission.

Quran 4:171 immediately guards the meaning: the Messiah is God's messenger, His word directed to Mary, and a spirit from Him; the same verse rejects saying "Three" and denies divine sonship. Quran 4:172 adds that the Messiah does not disdain to be God's servant, while Quran 5:75 places him in the line of messengers.

Islam therefore accepts the title without importing incarnation or atonement into it. Jesus is God's specially chosen Messiah, supported by miracles and sent to Israel. His greatness comes from God's choice, not from sharing God's being.

sections.title: The Gospels Give the Title a Wider Story
sections.body:
The New Testament openly identifies Jesus as Messiah. John 1:41 translates Messiah as Christ, Matthew 16:16 records Peter confessing Jesus as the Messiah, and John 4:25-26 presents Jesus accepting the title. Luke 4:18-21 connects his mission with anointing to preach good news and release.

Christians read the title within the wider New Testament and connect it to Jesus's divine sonship, death, resurrection, and future rule. Yet the word Messiah itself does not mean "God." The stronger Christian case must come from additional passages and theological claims.

That distinction matters because Muslims can affirm every text that calls Jesus Messiah while continuing to worship God alone.

sections.title: Does Islam Keep the Title but Empty Its Meaning?
sections.body:
A Christian may object that the Messiah's suffering, resurrection, and saving rule are not optional additions: they define how Jesus fulfills the role. Matthew 16:16's confession belongs to a Gospel with that wider account. Islam and Christianity do not mean exactly the same thing by confessing Jesus as Messiah.

The Muslim answer is that a mission is defined by God, not by everything later attached to its title. Quran 3:45 honors Jesus as Messiah; 4:171-172 simultaneously calls him messenger and servant and rejects divine sonship. Islam gives him a distinctive role without making atoning death or divine identity necessary to it. Accepting that correction requires reasons to trust the Quran, not wordplay.

sections.title: Do Not Ask a Title to Prove Too Much
sections.body:
Messiah does not mean 'God,' but neither does that linguistic point prove Jesus was only human. Titles must be read within the accounts that give them meaning.

The Quran does not provide one definitive explanation of the Arabic title's derivation; commentators offer several. It does give an unambiguous theological boundary: the Messiah does not disdain to be God's servant (4:172). That is the center of the Muslim case, not an unsupported reconstruction of a single uniform ancient Jewish expectation.

sections.title: Honor the One Whom God Chose
sections.body:
Islam does not ask anyone to abandon the Messiah. It asks people to understand his honor as the Quran and the prophetic pattern present it.

Jesus is God's chosen Messiah and faithful servant. Loving him means receiving his call to worship the one God who sent him.

sections.title: Love the Messiah in the Way His Mission Requires
sections.body:
The Islamic invitation keeps Jesus's unique honor while directing worship to the One who appointed him. This gives a seeker a positive way to believe in Jesus without accepting incarnation.

Read [The Crucifixion Question](/articles/the-crucifixion-question) next. There the disagreement about the Messiah's mission becomes most concrete, and the historical evidence must be faced honestly.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: Do Muslims believe Jesus is the Messiah?
A: Yes. The Quran itself names him al-Masih — the Messiah — and no other figure in the Quran bears this title. Affirming it is part of mainstream Islamic belief.

Q: Does the word “Messiah” itself mean “God”?
A: No. The Hebrew title means 'anointed one,' not 'God.' Christians base this particular Messiah's divine identity on a wider set of claims, so the word's meaning does not settle the whole debate.

Q: Why does the Quran call Jesus “a word from Him”?
A: Muslims understand this as pointing to Jesus’s miraculous origin — he was created by God’s direct command, without a father. The same verse that uses these exalted titles also insists that God is one (Quran 4:171), so “word” is an honor, not a claim that Jesus is an eternal divine person.

Q: Is the “false messiah” in Islamic teaching related to this title?
A: Islamic reports distinguish Jesus the Messiah from the deceiver called the Dajjal. Sahih Muslim 2937a describes their confrontation. The title alone does not establish divinity; the person and the mission must be identified from the sources.

Q: Do Muslims believe the Messiah will return?
A: Yes. Mainstream Islamic teaching connects Quran 4:159 and 43:61 with Jesus' return and relies on detailed reports including Sahih al-Bukhari 2476 and Sahih Muslim 2937a. The Quranic application is classical interpretation; the descent and Dajjal details come from hadith.

Q: Can someone accept Jesus as the Messiah without accepting the Trinity?
A: Yes: that is the Islamic position. The Quran both names Jesus as Messiah and rejects divine sonship in 4:171. Christians give the title a different theological setting, so agreement on the word should not hide disagreement about the mission.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
Selected sources and further reading:

- **The Muslim Jesus: Sayings and Stories in Islamic Literature** — Tarif Khalidi. A collection showing how deeply classical Islamic civilization revered Jesus.
- **The Islamic Jesus** — Mustafa Akyol. An accessible modern account of how Jesus is understood in Islam.
- **Jesus the Jew** — Geza Vermes. A classic historical study placing Jesus and his titles within first-century Judaism.
- **The Study Quran** — Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.).
- **Jesus: A Very Short Introduction** — Richard Bauckham. A concise statement of how mainstream Christian scholarship reads Jesus.

quranVerses.arabic: وَإِنَّهُۥ لَعِلْمٌۭ لِّلسَّاعَةِ فَلَا تَمْتَرُنَّ بِهَا وَٱتَّبِعُونِ ۚ هَٰذَا صِرَٰطٌۭ مُّسْتَقِيمٌۭ
quranVerses.translation: And indeed, Jesus will be [a sign for] knowledge of the Hour, so be not in doubt of it, and follow Me. This is a straight path.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: إِذْ قَالَتِ ٱلْمَلَٰٓئِكَةُ يَٰمَرْيَمُ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُبَشِّرُكِ بِكَلِمَةٍۢ مِّنْهُ ٱسْمُهُ ٱلْمَسِيحُ عِيسَى ٱبْنُ مَرْيَمَ وَجِيهًۭا فِى ٱلدُّنْيَا وَٱلْءَاخِرَةِ وَمِنَ ٱلْمُقَرَّبِينَ
quranVerses.translation: [And mention] when the angels said, "O Mary, indeed Allah gives you good tidings of a word from Him, whose name will be the Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary - distinguished in this world and the Hereafter and among those brought near [to Allah].
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: يَٰٓأَهْلَ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ لَا تَغْلُوا۟ فِى دِينِكُمْ وَلَا تَقُولُوا۟ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ إِلَّا ٱلْحَقَّ ۚ إِنَّمَا ٱلْمَسِيحُ عِيسَى ٱبْنُ مَرْيَمَ رَسُولُ ٱللَّهِ وَكَلِمَتُهُۥٓ أَلْقَىٰهَآ إِلَىٰ مَرْيَمَ وَرُوحٌۭ مِّنْهُ ۖ فَـَٔامِنُوا۟ بِٱللَّهِ وَرُسُلِهِۦ ۖ وَلَا تَقُولُوا۟ ثَلَٰثَةٌ ۚ ٱنتَهُوا۟ خَيْرًۭا لَّكُمْ ۚ إِنَّمَا ٱللَّهُ إِلَٰهٌۭ وَٰحِدٌۭ ۖ سُبْحَٰنَهُۥٓ أَن يَكُونَ لَهُۥ وَلَدٌۭ ۘ لَّهُۥ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ ۗ وَكَفَىٰ بِٱللَّهِ وَكِيلًۭا
quranVerses.translation: O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess in your religion or say about Allah except the truth. The Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary, was but a messenger of Allah and His word which He directed to Mary and a soul [created at a command] from Him. So believe in Allah and His messengers. And do not say, "Three"; desist - it is better for you. Indeed, Allah is but one God. Exalted is He above having a son. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: لَّن يَسْتَنكِفَ ٱلْمَسِيحُ أَن يَكُونَ عَبْدًۭا لِّلَّهِ وَلَا ٱلْمَلَٰٓئِكَةُ ٱلْمُقَرَّبُونَ ۚ وَمَن يَسْتَنكِفْ عَنْ عِبَادَتِهِۦ وَيَسْتَكْبِرْ فَسَيَحْشُرُهُمْ إِلَيْهِ جَمِيعًۭا
quranVerses.translation: Never would the Messiah disdain to be a servant of Allah, nor would the angels near [to Him]. And whoever disdains His worship and is arrogant - He will gather them to Himself all together.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: مَّا ٱلْمَسِيحُ ٱبْنُ مَرْيَمَ إِلَّا رَسُولٌۭ قَدْ خَلَتْ مِن قَبْلِهِ ٱلرُّسُلُ وَأُمُّهُۥ صِدِّيقَةٌۭ ۖ كَانَا يَأْكُلَانِ ٱلطَّعَامَ ۗ ٱنظُرْ كَيْفَ نُبَيِّنُ لَهُمُ ٱلْءَايَٰتِ ثُمَّ ٱنظُرْ أَنَّىٰ يُؤْفَكُونَ
quranVerses.translation: The Messiah, son of Mary, was not but a messenger; [other] messengers have passed on before him. And his mother was a supporter of truth. They both used to eat food. Look how We make clear to them the signs; then look how they are deluded.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: وَإِن مِّنْ أَهْلِ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ إِلَّا لَيُؤْمِنَنَّ بِهِۦ قَبْلَ مَوْتِهِۦ ۖ وَيَوْمَ ٱلْقِيَٰمَةِ يَكُونُ عَلَيْهِمْ شَهِيدًۭا
quranVerses.translation: And there is none from the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in Jesus before his death. And on the Day of Resurrection he will be against them a witness.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

bibleVerses.text: Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”
He first found his own brother, Simon, and said to him, “We have found the Messiah!” (which is, being interpreted, Christ).
The woman said to him, “I know that Messiah comes, he who is called Christ. When he has come, he will declare to us all things.” Jesus said to her, “I am he, the one who speaks to you.”

“The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent me to heal the broken hearted, to proclaim release to the captives, recovering of sight to the blind, to deliver those who are crushed, and to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord.” He closed the book, gave it back to the attendant, and sat down. The eyes of all in the synagogue were fastened on him. He began to tell them, “Today, this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”
